questions.question: For two positive real numbers \( x \) and \( y \), under what condition does A.M. \( = \) G.M. hold?
options: if and only if \( x = y \)
if and only if \( x + y = 0 \)
for all positive values of \( x \) and \( y \), always
questions.explanation: A.M. \( = \) G.M. exactly when \( x=y \): then \( \text{A.M.}=\frac{x+x}{2}=x \) and \( \text{G.M.}=\sqrt{x\cdot x}=x \), so both equal \( x \). For any \( x\neq y \), A.M. is strictly greater than G.M.
questions.hint: Try \( x=y \) in both formulas and see what happens; this is the only equality case for positive reals.
distractor_logic: mistakes the equality condition for \( x+y=0 \), which is also not possible for positive numbers
wrongly claims A.M. and G.M. are always equal, ignoring that A.M. \( > \) G.M. whenever \( x\neq y \)
confuses the equality condition with a symmetric-but-wrong condition \( x=-y \), which isn't meaningful for positive numbers

topics.name: Sequences and Arithmetic Progressions (A.P.)
topics.summary: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers that follows a definite rule, and each number in it is called a term. An Arithmetic Progression (A.P.) is a sequence in which every term after the first is obtained by adding a fixed number, called the common difference \( d \), to the term before it. If the first term is \( a \), the sequence looks like \( a, a+d, a+2d, a+3d, \ldots \), and its general (nth) term is \( a_n=a+(n-1)d \). The common difference can be positive (an increasing A.P.), negative (a decreasing A.P.), or zero (a constant sequence). Given any two terms of an A.P., \( d \) can be recovered by subtracting one term from the other and dividing by the gap between their positions. A.P.s describe situations of constant, steady change — equal salary increments, evenly spaced seating rows, or simple linear growth patterns — and correctly identifying \( a \) and \( d \) from the problem statement is the essential first step before applying any A.P. formula.
key_formulas: \( d = a_{n} - a_{n-1} \) (constant for every consecutive pair)
common_mistakes: using the exponent/multiplier \( n \) instead of \( n-1 \) when applying \( a_n=a+(n-1)d \)
making sign errors when \( d \) is negative (e.g. flipping the sign of the whole \( (n-1)d \) term)
being off by one when solving \( a+(n-1)d=\text{target} \) for \( n \) (forgetting the \( +1 \) after dividing)
assuming a number is a term of the A.P. without checking that \( (n-1) \) actually comes out to a non-negative integer

topics.name: Sum of n Terms of an A.P., Arithmetic Mean, and A.P. Properties
topics.summary: The sum of the first \( n \) terms of an A.P., written \( S_n \), can be found in two equivalent ways: \( S_n=\frac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d] \) when you know the first term and common difference, or \( S_n=\frac{n}{2}(a+l) \) when you know the first term \( a \) and last term \( l \). Both formulas come from pairing the first and last terms, the second and second-last terms, and so on — each pair adds up to the same total. The arithmetic mean (A.M.) of two numbers \( x \) and \( y \) is \( \frac{x+y}{2} \); more generally, inserting \( k \) evenly spaced arithmetic means between two numbers creates a longer A.P., and those \( k \) inserted means are symmetric about the A.M. of the two original numbers, so their sum is always \( k \) times that A.M. A useful property links sums and terms directly: if \( S_n \) is a quadratic expression \( An^2+Bn \) with no constant term, the underlying A.P. always has common difference \( d=2A \).
key_formulas: Sum of terms from position \( m+1 \) to \( n \): \( S_n - S_m \)
common_mistakes: using \( n \) instead of \( n-1 \) inside the bracket of \( S_n=\frac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d] \)
forgetting the \( \frac{1}{2} \) factor entirely when computing \( S_n \)

forgetting to divide by 2 when computing an arithmetic mean of two numbers

topics.name: Geometric Progressions (G.P.)
topics.summary: A Geometric Progression (G.P.) is a sequence in which every term after the first is obtained by multiplying the previous term by a fixed, non-zero number called the common ratio \( r \). If the first term is \( a \), the sequence is \( a, ar, ar^2, ar^3, \ldots \), and the general (nth) term is \( a_n=ar^{n-1} \). The ratio \( r \) can be found by dividing any term by the term immediately before it, and it stays constant throughout the whole sequence — unlike an A.P., where consecutive terms differ by a constant amount, consecutive G.P. terms differ by a constant factor. When \( r \) is negative, the terms alternate in sign, so it's important to track the sign of \( r^{n-1} \) carefully rather than working with \( |r| \). Three consecutive terms \( a,b,c \) of a G.P. always satisfy \( b^2=ac \) — the middle term is the geometric mean of the outer two — which is a defining algebraic property used throughout G.P. problems, from population growth to compound interest.
key_formulas: For 3 consecutive G.P. terms \( a,b,c \): \( b^2=ac \)
topics.worked_example: Find the 6th term of the G.P. \( 3, 6, 12, 24, \ldots \). Here \( a=3 \) and \( r=6/3=2 \). Using \( a_n=ar^{n-1} \): \( a_6=3\times 2^{5}=3\times 32=96 \).
common_mistakes: using the exponent \( n \) instead of \( n-1 \) when applying \( a_n=ar^{n-1} \)
dropping the sign of a negative common ratio and using \( |r| \) instead, which flips the sign of terms at odd positions

topics.name: Sum of n Terms of a G.P. (Finite and Infinite) and Geometric Mean
topics.summary: The sum of the first \( n \) terms of a G.P. is \( S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1} \) for \( r\neq 1 \); this formula divides by zero when \( r=1 \), so in that special case every term equals \( a \) and the sum is simply \( S_n=na \) instead. When \( |r|<1 \), the terms shrink toward zero as \( n \) grows, and the sum of infinitely many terms converges to a finite value: \( S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r} \), valid only under that \( |r|<1 \) condition. The geometric mean (G.M.) of two positive numbers \( x,y \) is \( \sqrt{xy} \); inserting one or more geometric means between two numbers extends them into a longer G.P., though unlike inserted arithmetic means, the sum of several inserted geometric means has no simple closed form and must be worked out from the common ratio directly. Infinite G.P. sums show up naturally in repeated-halving situations, such as a bouncing ball's ever-shrinking rebound heights adding up to a finite total distance.
topics.worked_example: Find the sum to infinity of the G.P. with \( a=8 \) and \( r=\frac{1}{2} \). Since \( |r|<1 \), \( S_\infty=\dfrac{8}{1-\frac{1}{2}}=\dfrac{8}{\frac{1}{2}}=16 \).

topics.name: Relationship Between A.M. and G.M.
topics.summary: For any two positive real numbers \( x \) and \( y \), the Arithmetic Mean \( \frac{x+y}{2} \) is always greater than or equal to the Geometric Mean \( \sqrt{xy} \); this is the A.M.-G.M. inequality, and equality holds only in the special case \( x=y \). The same idea extends to any number of positive reals — for three numbers \( x,y,z \), \( \frac{x+y+z}{3}\geq\sqrt[3]{xyz} \), again with equality only when all the numbers are equal. This inequality is a powerful shortcut in optimization problems: whenever a sum of positive quantities is fixed, their product is maximized exactly when the quantities are all equal, and whenever a product is fixed, the sum is minimized under the same condition. This principle explains, for instance, why a square encloses the maximum area among all rectangles of a given perimeter, and why an expression like \( x+\frac{k}{x} \) has a minimum value of \( 2\sqrt{k} \), achieved exactly when \( x=\sqrt{k} \).
key_formulas: Equality holds if and only if \( x=y \)
topics.worked_example: For \( x=2 \) and \( y=8 \): A.M. \( =\dfrac{2+8}{2}=5 \), G.M. \( =\sqrt{2\times 8}=\sqrt{16}=4 \). Indeed \( 5 \geq 4 \), confirming A.M. \( \geq \) G.M.

topics.name: Sum to n Terms of Special Series and Applications
topics.summary: Beyond A.P.s and G.P.s, three special series have their own standard closed-form sums: the sum of the first \( n \) natural numbers, \( \sum_{k=1}^{n}k=\frac{n(n+1)}{2} \); the sum of their squares, \( \sum_{k=1}^{n}k^2=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} \); and the sum of their cubes, \( \sum_{k=1}^{n}k^3=\left[\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right]^2 \) — notice this last one is simply the square of the first formula. More complicated series, such as \( \sum k(k+1) \), can usually be split into combinations of these three known sums using basic algebra. When a sum runs over a restricted range, such as \( \sum_{k=m}^{n}k \) rather than starting at 1, it's computed as the difference of two full sums, \( \sum_{k=1}^{n}k - \sum_{k=1}^{m-1}k \) — and getting that lower limit exactly right (\( m-1 \), not \( m \)) is essential. These formulas also model real counting problems, like the total number of items in a triangular stack.
common_mistakes: confusing the sum-of-squares formula \( \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} \) with the sum-of-cubes formula \( \left[\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right]^2 \)
using \( 2n-1 \) instead of \( 2n+1 \) in the sum-of-squares formula
getting an off-by-one wrong on the lower limit when computing a sum over a restricted range (using \( m \) instead of \( m-1 \))
forgetting one of the two parts when a series splits into a combination of standard sums, such as computing \( \sum k(k+1) \) as just \( \sum k^2 \) alone
